title: Electrolytes and Alcohol: Does Drinking Deplete Them?
excerpt: Does alcohol deplete electrolytes? Which minerals you lose, whether mixing Liquid IV or other powders into drinks is safe, if electrolytes change absorption, and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Does alcohol deplete electrolytes? Which minerals you lose, whether mixing Liquid IV into drinks is safe, and when electrolytes actually help.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, alcohol makes you lose some electrolytes, mainly because it makes you pee more and sometimes makes you sweat or throw up. For a typical social drinker after one night out, those losses are usually modest, and your kidneys correct them within a day once you eat and drink normally. Electrolyte drinks can help you rehydrate faster, especially if you were sick or sweaty, but they don't cure a hangover and they don't cancel out the alcohol. Mixing an electrolyte powder into your drink is generally fine for most healthy people, but it won't keep you sober, and it can make strong drinks easier to drink faster than you mean to.

**The quick rules:** Alternate alcoholic drinks with water or an electrolyte drink. Eat a real meal before you go out, because food does more for your electrolytes and your blood alcohol than any powder. Save most of your electrolytes for before bed and the next morning. Don't treat an electrolyte mixer as a reason to drink more. And if you have kidney disease, heart failure, or take blood pressure medicine, check with your doctor before using high-sodium or high-potassium products regularly.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article explains general research. It is not a substitute for a doctor who knows your health. **Get medical help if** you can't keep fluids down for more than about a day, you have severe muscle cramps or weakness, your heart is racing or skipping beats and it doesn't settle, you feel confused or unusually drowsy, you're barely peeing or your urine is very dark, or you faint. If someone who has been drinking is hard to wake, breathing slowly or irregularly, having a seizure, or vomiting while not fully awake, call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away. That is alcohol poisoning territory, not a hangover.

## What Electrolytes Actually Are

Electrolytes are minerals that carry an electric charge once they dissolve in your body's fluids. The main ones are **sodium, potassium, chloride, magnesium, calcium, phosphate, and bicarbonate**. They sound technical, but their jobs are everyday ones:

- **Sodium and chloride** hold water in your blood and the fluid around your cells. When people talk about "staying hydrated," sodium is doing most of the work.
- **Potassium** sits mostly inside your cells and helps nerves fire and muscles (including your heart) contract normally.
- **Magnesium** is involved in hundreds of chemical reactions, including muscle relaxation, nerve signalling, and energy production.
- **Calcium and phosphate** matter for muscles, nerves, and bones, and phosphate is part of how cells store energy.

Your kidneys keep all of these in a tight range. They decide, minute by minute, how much to hold on to and how much to let go in urine. That's why a healthy person can have a salty dinner one night and a bland one the next without their blood levels swinging wildly. Alcohol interferes with that control system for a while, which is where the electrolyte question comes from.

## Does Alcohol Deplete Electrolytes?

Yes, but how much depends a lot on how much you drink, how often, and what else happens during the night. It helps to separate three situations.

### 1. A normal night out

When you drink, alcohol suppresses a hormone called **vasopressin** (also called antidiuretic hormone, or ADH). Vasopressin normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, your kidneys let more water go, which is why you end up queuing for the bathroom more than the volume you drank would suggest. We cover that mechanism in detail in [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee).

This effect is strongest while your blood alcohol is rising. As it falls, the body tends to swing back the other way and conserve water. The urine you lose is mostly water, but it carries some sodium, potassium, and other minerals with it. Add a warm bar, dancing, and a few hours without much to eat, and you can wake up mildly dehydrated with slightly lower stores of some minerals.

For most healthy adults, that is a small, temporary dip. Researchers who have measured blood electrolytes in hungover volunteers have generally found that the changes are modest and don't line up well with how bad people say they feel. In other words, people with the worst hangovers aren't necessarily the ones with the most out-of-range electrolytes. That's an important clue, and we'll come back to it.

### 2. A night with vomiting or diarrhea

This changes things. Vomiting loses stomach acid, chloride, and potassium. Diarrhea loses water, sodium, potassium, and bicarbonate. A night that ends with being sick, or a morning spent in the bathroom, is the situation where electrolyte losses become real and where an oral rehydration drink earns its place. If that sounds familiar, our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers what's going on and when to worry.

### 3. Regular heavy drinking

This is a genuinely different problem. People who drink heavily over weeks, months, or years commonly develop low magnesium, low potassium, low phosphate, and sometimes low sodium. The causes pile up: alcohol increases the loss of magnesium and other minerals through the kidneys, heavy drinkers often eat less, and the gut absorbs nutrients less well. These deficits are well documented in medical literature on alcohol use and are something doctors check for with blood tests. They are not something a sports drink fixes, and correcting them sometimes needs supervised treatment.

There's also a less common pattern sometimes called **"beer potomania,"** where someone drinks large amounts of beer while eating very little. Beer is mostly water with very little sodium, so blood sodium can fall to dangerously low levels. It's rare in social drinkers, but it's a good reminder that the problem isn't always "too little fluid." Sometimes it's too much plain fluid without enough salt or food.

## Which Electrolytes Alcohol Affects Most

Here's a plain summary of what's known for each mineral. The numbers vary a lot between people, so think of this as direction rather than precise amounts.

| Electrolyte | What alcohol does | Matters most for |
|---|---|---|
| **Sodium** | Some lost in extra urine and sweat; vomiting adds to losses | Feeling thirsty, lightheaded, or flat the next day |
| **Potassium** | Lost in urine, vomit, and diarrhea | Muscle weakness, cramps, heart rhythm (mainly with heavy losses) |
| **Magnesium** | Alcohol increases kidney losses; low levels common with heavy drinking | Cramps, twitching, poor sleep, heart rhythm in heavy drinkers |
| **Phosphate** | Low levels common in heavy, long-term drinking | Weakness; a medical concern mainly in heavy drinkers |
| **Zinc** | Increased urinary loss with regular drinking | Long-term nutrition rather than next-day symptoms |
| **Calcium** | Can fall alongside low magnesium | Mostly relevant in chronic heavy drinking |

Magnesium gets the most attention online, partly for good reason. If you want the detail, our page on [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers what the research says, who might benefit from a supplement, and who should be careful.

## Are Hangovers Caused by Electrolyte Loss?

Mostly no. This is the most common misunderstanding about electrolytes and alcohol, and it's worth being direct about.

Dehydration and mineral loss contribute to some hangover symptoms: thirst, dry mouth, a dull headache, and feeling lightheaded when you stand up. But a hangover is a bigger package. Researchers now think the main drivers include:

- **Inflammation.** Alcohol triggers an immune response, and markers of inflammation rise during a hangover.
- **Acetaldehyde.** This is the toxic first by-product your liver makes when it breaks down alcohol.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol can help you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night.
- **Low blood sugar and stomach irritation.** These add to the shaky, queasy feeling.
- **Congeners.** These are other compounds in drinks, especially dark spirits and red wine, that seem to make hangovers worse.

As mentioned above, studies that measure electrolytes in hungover people generally haven't found a strong link between electrolyte levels and hangover severity. That's why you can drink plenty of water and still feel terrible, and why electrolyte drinks help some people a lot and others barely at all. They fix the fluid part. They don't touch the rest.

So a fair way to think about electrolytes is this: they are a useful piece of recovery, especially after a sweaty or sick night, but there is no good evidence that electrolyte drinks prevent hangovers on their own.

## Mixing Electrolytes With Alcohol: Liquid IV, Powders, and Mixers

A lot of people now stir an electrolyte powder into vodka, tequila, or a seltzer, on the theory that they'll rehydrate as they go. Here's what that actually does and doesn't do.

### Is it safe to mix Liquid IV or other electrolyte powders with alcohol?

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no known harmful chemical reaction between the salts and sugars in electrolyte powders and alcohol. A packet in a cocktail is, chemically, just a salty-sweet mixer.

The caveats are practical rather than chemical:

- **It doesn't reduce your blood alcohol.** The alcohol is absorbed and processed exactly as it would be otherwise. Your liver works at its own pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many people, and no powder speeds that up.
- **It can make strong drinks go down easier.** A sweet, flavored mixer hides the taste of alcohol. That makes it easy to drink faster than you planned, which matters far more for how you feel tomorrow than a few hundred milligrams of sodium.
- **The extra salt and sugar add up.** One packet is fine. Three or four over a night, on top of salty bar food, is a lot of sodium for anyone watching their blood pressure, and the sugar adds calories.
- **It isn't as hydrating as it sounds.** An electrolyte drink mixed with alcohol still contains alcohol, which still suppresses vasopressin. A separate glass of water or plain electrolyte drink between rounds does more for hydration than the same powder mixed into the alcohol.

If you like the taste, using an electrolyte powder as a mixer is fine. Just treat it as a mixer, not as protection. Our [Liquid IV for hangovers](/never-hungover/liquid-iv-for-hangover) page looks at that product specifically, including what's in it and who it suits.

### Do electrolytes make you absorb alcohol faster?

There's no good evidence that electrolytes themselves speed up alcohol absorption. Alcohol doesn't need a carrier to get into your blood. It passes through the lining of your stomach and small intestine on its own, and most of it is absorbed in the small intestine.

What does change how fast alcohol hits you is mostly about your stomach:

- **Food is the big one.** A meal slows how quickly your stomach empties into your small intestine, which slows and lowers the peak of your blood alcohol.
- **Carbonation may speed things up a little.** Some studies suggest fizzy drinks can lead to faster absorption in some people, though results are mixed. Bubbles may nudge alcohol along a bit faster, but food matters much more.
- **Sugar-free mixers may raise blood alcohol slightly.** A study by Cecile Marczinski and Amy Stamates, published in *Alcoholism: Clinical and Experimental Research* in 2013, found that people who drank vodka with a diet mixer reached higher breath alcohol levels than when they had the same vodka with a sugar-sweetened mixer. The likely reason is that sugar slows stomach emptying a little.

That last point matters for electrolyte mixers because many of them come in both regular and sugar-free versions. A sugar-free electrolyte mixer isn't dangerous, but it won't slow absorption the way a sugary one might, and it certainly won't slow it as much as eating dinner.

### What about "alcoholic electrolyte drinks" and electrolyte hard seltzers?

A growing number of canned drinks now combine alcohol with added electrolytes, and some marketing hints that they'll leave you feeling better the next day. A few things to keep in mind:

- **The alcohol is still the main ingredient that matters.** A hard seltzer with added electrolytes has the same alcohol as any other drink of the same strength and size. Check the ABV and can size, because some are stronger than a regular beer.
- **The electrolyte amounts are often small.** Many contain far less sodium than an oral rehydration drink. They're not a substitute for a real rehydration drink the next morning.
- **There's no good evidence that they reduce hangovers.** We're not aware of independent research showing that electrolyte-added alcoholic drinks cause milder hangovers than the same amount of alcohol without them.

If you like them, enjoy them as a drink. Just count them the same way you'd count any other drink.

## When Electrolytes Actually Help After Drinking

Even though electrolytes aren't a hangover cure, there are times when they're clearly worth using.

**You were sick.** Vomiting or diarrhea is the clearest case. An oral rehydration solution, which has a specific balance of sodium and glucose designed for absorption, replaces fluid faster than plain water. Pedialyte and similar products are built on this idea.

**You were sweating a lot.** A hot summer day, a festival, a dance floor, or a sauna on top of drinking means you're losing salt through sweat as well as urine.

**You're thirsty, lightheaded, and peeing very little.** These are classic signs of mild dehydration. A drink with some sodium will help your body hold on to the fluid instead of passing it straight through.

**You can't face food yet.** Food is usually the best source of electrolytes, but if you're too queasy to eat, a drink with salt and a little sugar is a reasonable bridge until you can.

For a side-by-side look at specific brands and how their sodium and sugar compare, see our guide to [the best electrolyte drinks for a hangover](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared). If you'd rather make your own, a basic home mix of water, a pinch of salt, a little sugar, and some citrus works for most people.

## Timing: Before, During, or After?

Timing matters more than most people think, and we have a whole page on it: [electrolytes before or after drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking). The short version:

- **Before:** arrive normally hydrated and fed. There's no benefit to "pre-loading" large amounts of electrolytes, and a big salty drink before you go out mostly just makes you thirsty.
- **During:** a glass of water or a plain electrolyte drink between alcoholic drinks slows your pace and replaces some fluid.
- **Before bed:** one of the most useful windows. A glass of water or an electrolyte drink before sleep helps you start the morning less dry.
- **The morning after:** drink steadily rather than gulping, eat something with salt and potassium (eggs, toast, a banana, soup, or a salty breakfast), and add an electrolyte drink if you were sick or sweaty.

## Food Beats Powders for Most People

It's easy to forget that ordinary food is full of electrolytes. A typical breakfast covers a lot of what a packet would:

- **Sodium:** eggs, toast, soup, broth, salted crackers, a breakfast sandwich.
- **Potassium:** bananas, potatoes, avocado, yogurt, orange juice, coconut water.
- **Magnesium:** nuts, seeds, whole grains, leafy greens, dark chocolate.

Food also brings carbohydrates, which help with the shaky, low-energy feeling, and it gives your stomach something to work on. If you can eat, eating plus water does most of what a commercial electrolyte drink would do. The drinks are most useful when you can't eat, when you were sick, or when you just find a cold, salty drink more appealing than a glass of water. All of those are reasonable reasons to use one.

## Who Should Be Careful With Electrolyte Drinks and Alcohol

Electrolyte drinks are safe for most healthy adults, but they're not free of risk for everyone.

- **Kidney disease.** Your kidneys are what normally clear extra potassium and sodium. If they don't work well, products high in potassium or sodium can push levels too high. Ask your doctor before using them.
- **Heart failure or high blood pressure.** Many electrolyte drinks and powders contain several hundred to over a thousand milligrams of sodium per serving. That can matter if you've been told to limit salt.
- **Blood pressure and heart medicines.** Some medicines, including ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and potassium-sparing diuretics, can raise potassium levels. Combining them with high-potassium supplements or salt substitutes is something to check with a pharmacist or doctor.
- **Diabetes.** Sugary electrolyte drinks affect blood sugar, and alcohol itself can cause low blood sugar later in the night. Sugar-free versions or a planned approach with your care team make sense.
- **Regular heavy drinking.** If you drink heavily most days, low magnesium, potassium, and phosphate are common and can be serious. A sports drink won't correct them properly. A doctor can check your levels with a simple blood test.

### The opposite problem: drinking too much plain water

Most people drink too little after a night out, but it's possible to overdo it. Drinking very large amounts of plain water in a short time, especially after losing salt through sweat or vomiting, can dilute your blood sodium. This is uncommon, but it's one reason a drink with some salt, or a salty snack alongside your water, is a sensible choice when you're rehydrating after a big loss of fluid.

## Signs Your Electrolytes Might Actually Be Off

A normal hangover can make you tired, headachy, and thirsty. Those alone don't mean your electrolytes are dangerously low. These signs deserve more attention, especially if they're strong or getting worse:

- Muscle cramps, twitching, or weakness that doesn't fade as the day goes on
- A racing, pounding, or irregular heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest and fluids
- Confusion, unusual drowsiness, or trouble concentrating that seems out of proportion
- Vomiting or diarrhea that stops you from keeping fluids down for around a day
- Very little urine, or very dark urine, despite drinking
- Fainting or nearly fainting when you stand up

If you notice these, see a doctor or urgent care. A blood test can show whether your sodium, potassium, or magnesium is off, and treatment is straightforward when it's caught. If someone shows signs of alcohol poisoning (hard to wake, slow or irregular breathing, seizures, blue-tinged lips, vomiting while not fully conscious), call emergency services rather than trying to treat it with fluids at home.

## Where DHM Fits, Honestly

Electrolytes address the fluid side of drinking. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that people take for a different reason: research, much of it in animals, suggests it may affect how the body processes alcohol and how alcohol acts on the brain. Human data is still limited, and there is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers or protects you from the effects of heavy drinking. It does nothing for electrolytes either.

Some people use both as part of a routine: water and a real meal, a glass of water between drinks, DHM with their last drink or before bed, and an electrolyte drink or salty breakfast in the morning. If you want to try DHM, [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines 1,000 mg of DHM with a few supporting ingredients including some electrolytes, and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a simpler, lower-cost option. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts. None of these products make it safe to drink more than you otherwise would.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol does cause some electrolyte loss, mostly through extra urine, sweat, and especially vomiting or diarrhea. After a normal night, the loss is usually small and your body fixes it within a day once you eat and drink. Electrolyte drinks help most when you were sick or sweaty, or when you can't face food. Mixing an electrolyte powder into your drink is fine for most healthy people, but it doesn't lower your blood alcohol or protect you from a hangover, and it can make strong drinks easier to overdo. Food, pacing, and water between drinks still do the heavy lifting. If you have kidney or heart problems, take blood pressure medicine, or drink heavily most days, talk to your doctor about electrolytes rather than relying on packets.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol deplete electrolytes?**

Yes, to a degree. Alcohol suppresses the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more and lose some sodium, potassium, and magnesium along with the fluid. Sweating, vomiting, or diarrhea add to the losses. After a normal night out the drop is usually small and corrects itself within a day. Regular heavy drinking is different and commonly leads to low magnesium, potassium, and phosphate that need medical attention.

**Can you mix Liquid IV with alcohol?**

For most healthy adults, yes. There's no harmful chemical reaction between electrolyte powders and alcohol. But mixing it in doesn't lower your blood alcohol or prevent a hangover, and the sweet flavor can make strong drinks easy to drink quickly. You'll get more hydration benefit from drinking the electrolyte drink separately, between alcoholic drinks or before bed.

**Do electrolytes make you get drunk faster?**

There's no good evidence that electrolytes themselves speed up alcohol absorption. What matters most is whether you've eaten, how fast you drink, and how strong the drinks are. One study found that sugar-free mixers led to higher breath alcohol than sugary ones, likely because sugar slows stomach emptying a little, so a sugar-free electrolyte mixer won't slow absorption the way food does.

**Should I drink electrolytes before or after drinking alcohol?**

The most useful times are between drinks, before bed, and the next morning. Pre-loading electrolytes before you go out has little benefit if you're already normally hydrated. Eating a proper meal before drinking does more to protect you than any drink you take beforehand.

**Are electrolyte drinks a hangover cure?**

No. They help with the dehydration part of a hangover, which covers thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache and lightheadedness. Most hangover symptoms come from other things, including inflammation, poor sleep, acetaldehyde, and low blood sugar. Research has generally not found a strong link between electrolyte levels and how bad a hangover feels.

**Which electrolyte does alcohol deplete the most?**

In a single night, the biggest losses are usually water and sodium, with potassium added if you vomit or have diarrhea. With regular heavy drinking, magnesium is one of the most commonly depleted minerals, along with potassium and phosphate. A doctor can check these with a blood test if you're worried.

**Do alcoholic electrolyte drinks or electrolyte hard seltzers prevent hangovers?**

There's no good evidence that they do. The alcohol content is what drives a hangover, and the electrolyte amounts in these drinks are often small. Count them the same as any other drink of the same strength, and still drink water between rounds.

**Is it possible to have too many electrolytes after drinking?**

For healthy adults, it's unusual, because the kidneys clear the extra. It's a real concern for people with kidney disease, heart failure, or those taking medicines that raise potassium, such as ACE inhibitors or potassium-sparing diuretics. If that applies to you, check with your doctor before using high-sodium or high-potassium products.
